notes:
I've written notes for every verse, but some areas are thin. I found almost nothing on vv. 5–7 or vv. 11–21 beyond Enduring Word and Precept Austin. Nothing I read came from an Orthodox or Pentecostal writer, from the NET Bible notes or Bible Odyssey, or from word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. Those are left out rather than guessed. Enduring Word, Bible.org and Catholic Answers pages are full articles I read. Everything else comes from search-result excerpts.

**v. 1**
- Paul's love for his people turns into action: he doesn't just care, he prays. He takes no pleasure in Israel having stumbled (9:32). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 2**
- "Zeal without knowledge" describes Paul himself before Damascus. Guzik warns that sincere Christians can have the same problem: lots of zeal, little knowledge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 3**
- Guzik says the problem was moral as well as mental. Israel didn't just lack information; it refused to submit. Information alone saves no one. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- Gotquestions agrees: It is failure to submit to God's righteousness. This is a spiritual and moral failure rather than an intellectual one. https://www.gotquestions.org/Christ-is-the-end-of-the-law.html
- Guzik adds that Paul's teaching on election in chapter 9 does not cancel human responsibility. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 4: "end" (Greek *telos*) – commentators really differ here**
- The Pulpit Commentary notes the word could mean (1) termination, (2) fulfilment, (3) aim or purpose. https://biblehub.com/romans/10-4.htm
- **Ending.** Ellicott reads it as termination: Christ ends the law's work by replacing it (https://biblehub.com/romans/10-4.htm). Meyer says this reading, which follows Augustine, is held by most of the modern expositors (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/10-4.htm).
- **Aim or purpose.** Barnes says purpose is doubtless its meaning here (https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/10-4.htm). Calvin (Reformed) says everything the law teaches, commands or promises has always a reference to Christ as its main object (https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-4.html).
- **Fulfilment.** Gill (Baptist) prefers the "fulfilling end": Christ kept the law perfectly and brought in a righteousness that counts before God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-4.html
- **Spurgeon (Baptist)** combines the views. Christ is the law's great purpose, and he also ends its penalty and curse for believers. Christ did not come to make the law milder. https://www.spurgeon.org/sermons/christ-the-end-of-the-law
- **Guzik's balance.** The law ends as the basis of our relationship with God. It does not end as God's standard or as the thing that shows our need of a Saviour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- **Methodist and Wesleyan.** Clarke reads it through sacrifice: Christ was the real offering the law's sacrifices pointed to. Where the law ends, Christ begins. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/lit/romans/10-4.html
  - Benson says the righteousness meant here includes justification and also sanctification and the obedience that follows. https://mail.biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/10-4.htm
- **Lutheran.** A 1517 article says Christ took upon Himself to obey the law. His obedience is credited to us already. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-romans-10-8b-13-lent-1-series-c

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the law's path is plain. If you want life through the law, you must keep all of it, perfectly. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**vv. 6–7**
- Guzik: we don't have to climb to heaven or go down to the abyss to get Jesus. We believe and receive. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- Catholic reading (Hahn and Mitch, *Ignatius Catholic Study Bible*, quoted by Catholic Answers): these verses are an "interpretive paraphrase" of Deuteronomy 30:12–14. Just as Israel couldn't say the Torah was out of reach, it can't say the gospel is. The gospel has reached Israel's doorstep. https://www.catholic.com/qa/what-is-the-complete-meaning-of-romans-109-10

**v. 8**
- Clarke: There is no occasion to seek high or low for the saving power; the word of reconciliation is nigh. The way of salvation is now both plain and easy. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-8.html
- Calvin: Paul doesn't exclude the law's commands. His point is that forgiveness of sins counts as righteousness even without the strict obedience the law demands. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-8.html
- Lutheran (1517): the word of faith is the Word that declares us righteous and gives us Christ's own righteousness as a gift. It creates and sustains faith. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-romans-10-8b-13-lent-1-series-c

**v. 9**
- **"Jesus is Lord."** Robertson, quoted by Guzik: no Jew would say this unless he really trusted Christ, since *Kurios* (Lord) is used of God in the Greek Old Testament. No Gentile would say it while still worshipping the emperor as lord. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- Gotquestions links "Lord" to Yahweh in Joel 2:32, quoted in v. 13. https://www.gotquestions.org/confess-with-your-mouth.html
- **The resurrection.** Guzik says believing the resurrection includes the work of the cross rather than replacing it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- **Why "mouth" comes before "heart."** Several commentators say Paul is following the order of Deuteronomy. In real experience, faith comes before confession. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/10-9.htm
- Ellicott calls this the earliest formal confession of faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/10-9.htm

**vv. 9–10: is confession a condition of salvation? – the main dividing point**
- **Confession as evidence (evangelical).** Gotquestions says confession is best read as an evidence of salvation, rather than the condition itself.
  - It also warns against "decisional regeneration," meaning treating a sinner's prayer as what saves. https://www.gotquestions.org/confess-with-your-mouth.html
  - Precept Austin takes the same view (citing MacDonald and others). https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_108-11
- **Reformed.** Calvin says confession is not the cause of salvation. Paul is describing true faith, which shows itself in confession. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-10.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** By faith alone we are justified; but by confession in actual life, which is the fruit of faith, our salvation is secured. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-10.html
- **Wesley's Notes:** believing "with the heart" means "not the understanding only." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-10.html
- **Free Grace vs. Lordship Salvation.** A Grace Evangelical Society article on Bible.org criticises the common readings.
  - It notes that John MacArthur, a Lordship Salvation teacher, calls this passage one of the clearest statements of how to be saved.
  - Its own argument: "justified" (v. 10a) happens by faith alone. "Saved" here means a different, later deliverance that comes with confession, so public confession is not needed to get to heaven. https://bible.org/article/why-confess-christ-use-and-abuse-romans-109-10
- **Churches of Christ.** Coffman reads the confession as the one made before baptism. He treats faith, repentance, confession and baptism all as required for salvation. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/romans/10-9.html
- **Catholic.**
  - Catholic Answers says these verses don't support "once saved, always saved." It points to Romans 2:6–7 to argue that good works in Christ play a part in salvation. https://www.catholic.com/qa/what-is-the-complete-meaning-of-romans-109-10
  - A second Catholic Answers article says belief and confession are necessary, but the whole witness of the New Testament shows us that baptism is necessary as well. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/baptism-saves-you

**v. 11**
- Spurgeon (quoted by Guzik) thinks "the Scripture says" points to the general teaching of several passages, not one verse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 12**
- Guzik: both Jews and Greeks tended to credit their birth or nation. Paul rules out salvation on that basis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 13**
- Guzik: read Romans 9 alone and salvation looks like all God's doing. Read Romans 10 alone and it looks like all ours. Together we see both sides. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- Gotquestions: Paul applies a verse about Yahweh (Joel 2:32) to Jesus. https://www.gotquestions.org/confess-with-your-mouth.html

**vv. 14–15**
- Guzik: God could have used angels, but his normal way is preaching. Preachers must be sent by God and by the church. Their feet are "beautiful" because they work with God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- Lutheran (1517): we preach faith into their ears and hearts until it flows out of their mouths as a confession. https://www.1517.org/articles/epistle-romans-10-8b-13-lent-1-series-c

**v. 16**
- Guzik: if salvation is this simple, why is Israel set aside? Because many did not believe the message (Isaiah 53:1). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 17**
- Guzik: Israel heard but did not believe, which makes them (and us) more responsible. Morris notes that ordinary first-century people heard rather than read. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
- A writer quoted on Precept Austin calls it a (supernatural) "quickened" word, that creates (life giving) living faith, and sees here the root of the missionary urge. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1016-21

**v. 18**
- Bruce (via Guzik): "all the earth" isn't exaggeration. The gospel had reached most of the Mediterranean world where Jews lived, which is all the argument needs. Clarke: if the Jews did not believe, the fault was their own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 19**
- Guzik: God warned (Deuteronomy 32:21) that he would draw others close and make Israel jealous. Israel ignored that too. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 20**
- Guzik: Israel's rejection of its own Messiah is strange, but Isaiah foretold it, so it didn't surprise God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/

**v. 21**
- Guzik: this is God's verdict on a Messiah-rejecting Israel. It is heavier because of how much Israel had been given. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-10/
